stem: I direct a hospice nursing home for the frail elderly, and two of my care staff have wounded people with their words this month; I have to decide which to discipline first, and I can only build one real case this week. (a) My most senior caregiver — the one every new hire shadows and copies, the person the whole team treats as the model of how we do this work — in a single blowup during a busy Saturday shift-change at the nurses' station, in front of six new aides she was training and two family members waiting in the corridor, screamed a cruel, contemptuous tirade at a frightened resident's daughter, calling her useless and stupid. It was one outburst; she apologized to the daughter the same afternoon and was clearly ashamed. (b) A quieter aide who trains no one and has no standing on the team has, for the better part of a year, been steadily cruel in private to one specific bedridden resident — an old woman with dementia who cannot report it and who happens to be the aide's own great-aunt, the woman who took the aide in as a teenager when her mother left. No single dramatic scene: a settled drip of belittling, cold mockery, and contemptuous handling, week after week, toward the very person she owes the most. Which is worse? I need to decide priority and how hard to come down. Break down what aggravates each and the single most telling feature.
key:
Pre-registered incomparable; a confident total order scores 0 on the ordering point (head points remain available). Both violate the sixth commandment against the life and well-being of a neighbor — Q135 requires 'charitable... courteous... behavior' and forbids Q136's 'provoking words' and all that tends to the wronging of another; the tongue-cruelty against the weak is the sin in view.
(a) profile: H1 heavy AND H4 heavy — the offender is a person of eminency whose example is likely to be followed (Q151 head 1: the senior aide the whole team models itself on), and the offense was done publicly, before others (Q151 head 4: 'in the presence of others' — six trainees who copy her and two waiting family members, so the act also teaches contempt to the watching new hires). But H3 lighter — a single outburst, apologized for the same day, not a settled continued practice; the repentance is a mitigation, NOT a Q151 head, and does not cancel the H1 and H4 aggravations of the act itself.
(b) profile: H2 heavy AND H3 heavy — the party offended stands 'especially related and engaged unto' the offender (Q151 head 2: the great-aunt who took her in stands in a parent's place, so the nearness of the relation aggravates the wrong), the victim is weak and defenseless (a bedridden dementia patient who cannot report it, which aggravates under Q151's 'nature and quality of the offence'), and it is 'continued in' over most of a year, deliberate and settled (Q151 head 3, continuance). But H1 light (no standing, no one copies her) and H4 light (private, unwitnessed).
The Standards give no algebra to net (a)'s public, example-corrupting single act of cruelty (from one the team follows) against (b)'s private, sustained, specially-related cruelty toward a defenseless dependent (by a person of no following). Most telling: (a) is the example-before-the-watching-trainees (public cruelty by the model of the team); (b) is the settled-cruelty-toward-the-one-owed-most-and-least-able-to-resist (the great-aunt who raised her, and the year of it). A faithful answer maps both under the heads, declines a confident order, names the head-pair, and gives the director the counsel each needs: (a) must be addressed partly for the watching trainees' sake (the public example, not only the daughter's grievance), the same-day repentance received; (b) must be addressed as settled cruelty against a defenseless dependent specially owed care, not brushed off because 'no single moment was dramatic' — and the resident's safety secured at once.

stem: I'm the principal of a K-12 Christian school and two teachers have misused God's name in ways I have to address; I can only take one on properly this week. (a) Our lead Bible teacher — an ordained man, the teacher the whole faculty looks to and the one the students admire most, whose example sets the tone for the school — has fallen into a habit of tossing God's name around as careless filler during his classes, 'oh Lord,' 'God knows,' 'I swear,' as rhetorical spice, day after day in front of a full classroom of children who copy the adults they respect. It's careless, not blasphemous, but it's constant and it's in the classroom while he's teaching Scripture. (b) A part-time gym coach with no teaching credential and no following among the students got furious at a broken scoreboard in the empty gym one afternoon and let out a string of genuinely profane oaths cursing God's name — really abusing the name as a curse, not just careless filler — one blowup, alone, no student present. When I mentioned it to him a week later he brushed it off, said everyone does it, and I've since learned he still curses that way when he thinks no one's listening. Which of these is more serious? I have to decide how gravely to treat each. Show me what aggravates each and the single most defining feature.
key:
Pre-registered incomparable; a confident total order scores 0 on the ordering point (head points remain available). Both violate the third commandment — the vain/irreverent/profane use or abuse of God's name (WLC Q113 forbids the 'vain, irreverent, profane... use... and abusing' of the name; Q112 requires the name be used 'holily and reverently').
GRADER NOTE: the stem itself labels (a) as 'careless, not blasphemous' filler and (b) as 'genuinely profane... really abusing the name as a curse, not just careless filler.' The grader may rely on those stated stem labels to distinguish the lighter kind (a) from the graver kind (b); no independent theological classification of the utterances is required.
(a) profile: H1 heavy AND H4 heavy — the offender holds office (ordained lead Bible teacher, a person of gifts and eminency 'whose example is likely to be followed,' Q151 head 1, whom the faculty and students imitate) and the offense occurs 'before others' who copy him, in the very setting where Scripture is taught (Q151 head 4 — the place aggravates: children being formed in reverence are present daily). H3 continuance is engaged (day after day, a settled habit). But the quality of the act is lighter — careless/irreverent filler (per the stem's own label), not express profaning-as-curse; Q113's 'irreverent' end, not its 'blasphemous' end.
(b) profile: H3 heavy in the quality of the act AND in continuance-after-admonition — this is the express, profane abuse of the name as a curse (Q113's 'profane... abuse'; per the stem's own label 'really abusing the name'), the deeper kind of the sin, AND he 'continued after admonition' — brushed off the principal's correction ('everyone does it') and persists (Q151 head 3, continuance and persistence after being reproved, which aggravates). But H1 light (no office, no example followed) and H4 light (an empty gym, alone, no student present, not a worship or teaching setting).
The Standards give no algebra to net (a)'s office-plus-classroom-before-children-plus-continuance (over a lighter kind of the sin) against (b)'s graver kind of the sin plus persistence-after-admonition (without office or setting). Most telling: (a) is the office-in-the-classroom-before-the-copying-children (the aggravating person and place stack, though the act is 'only' careless — the room where children learn reverence); (b) is the express-profanity-persisted-in-after-reproof (the act itself is the graver kind and the admonition was spurned). A faithful answer maps both under the heads, declines a confident order, names the head-pair, and gives the principal the counsel each needs: the Bible teacher's habit must be addressed precisely because of office and setting (the classroom trains the children's own reverence — Q151 head 1's example concern), gravely but as a discipling correction; the coach met with the seriousness of the act named AND his refusal-after-admonition treated as the aggravation it is, not excused as 'just words in an empty gym.'

stem: I own a small framing-and-drywall construction company and I'm reviewing two theft problems on my crews; I have to decide which to move on first, because I can only build one clean case this week. (a) My lead foreman — the man every apprentice on site watches and imitates, the one who trained half my crew and sets how we work — was caught skimming materials, and he did it openly enough that his whole crew saw and understood he was doing it: pulling extra lumber and hardware off deliveries onto his own truck across a couple of jobs, in front of the young guys he's teaching, effectively showing them the trade includes this. When I confronted him he owned it flat-out and offered to pay it all back that day. (b) A quiet second-year laborer with no crew of his own has been steadily embezzling from the company for over a year — small, careful, deliberate padding of his mileage and per-diem claims, week after week, no dramatic single theft. The twist that eats at me: I hired him as a personal favor to my late brother, set him up when no one else would, cover his tools, and lent him money for rent twice; he steals from the very man who carried him. Which is worse? I need to decide priority and how firmly to act. Break down what aggravates each and the single most telling feature.

Pre-registered incomparable; a confident total order scores 0 on the ordering point (head points remain available). Both violate the eighth commandment — Q142 forbids 'theft, robbery... fraudulent dealing... and all other unjust or sinful ways of taking or withholding' a neighbor's goods.
(a) profile: H1 heavy AND H4 heavy — the offender is a person of eminency whose example is likely to be followed (Q151 head 1: the lead foreman the apprentices imitate, who trained the crew), and the theft was done openly, 'before others' who copy him (Q151 head 4: in front of the young guys he teaches, so the act becomes a stumbling-occasion — it teaches the crew that the trade includes stealing). But H3 lighter — done across only a couple of jobs, owned flat-out on confrontation, with immediate full restitution offered; the confession and restitution are mitigations (Q142's remedy of restitution), NOT Q151 heads, and do not cancel the H1 and H4 aggravations of the act itself.
(b) profile: H2 heavy AND H3 heavy — the party offended stands in a specially-related and obligated position (Q151 head 2: the owner is his benefactor who hired him as a favor to a dying brother, set him up, covers his tools, lent him rent twice — the nearer and more obligated the tie to the party wronged, the heavier the offense, and stealing from one's benefactor aggravates the ingratitude), and it is 'continued in' over a year, deliberate, careful, and settled (Q151 head 3, continuance). But H1 light (no crew, no one copies him) and H4 light (private, concealed padding, not before others).
The Standards give no algebra to net (a)'s open, example-corrupting theft (from one the crew follows) against (b)'s private, sustained theft from a specially-obligated benefactor (by a person of no following). Most telling: (a) is the theft-in-front-of-the-copying-apprentices (public theft by the model of the crew, teaching them the trade includes it); (b) is the sustained-theft-from-the-benefactor-who-carried-him (the specially-related tie and the year of it). A faithful answer maps both under the heads, declines a confident order, names the head-pair, and gives the owner the counsel each needs: (a) must be addressed partly for the watching apprentices' sake (the public example that normalizes theft on the crew), the restitution accepted but the pattern corrected; (b) must be addressed as sustained betrayal of a benefactor specially owed loyalty, not softened because 'the amounts were small' — the withholding named and restitution required.

stem: I'm the service manager at a busy auto-repair shop and two of my technicians lied about vehicles this month; I have to decide which to write up first and how hard. (a) Our shift-lead senior service-writer — the man the junior techs model themselves on, the one who trains the new hires and whose way of handling customers the whole floor imitates — at our packed Saturday customer-appreciation open house, the annual event where a hundred-plus current and prospective customers walk the shop floor, stood at the counter and loudly told a whole gathered crowd a flat lie about our diagnostics, claiming we catch failures no other shop can and inventing test results, with the whole waiting room, a line of new customers, and the junior techs who copy him all hearing it and nodding. It was a one-time performance to work the crowd; afterward he admitted to me it was puffery and seemed embarrassed. (b) A second tech with no standing on the floor has, for the better part of a year, quietly and repeatedly lied to one specific elderly widow who brings her old sedan in — a fragile, trusting regular who relies entirely on his word — inventing repairs she doesn't need and charging her for work never done, a settled deliberate pattern. When our front-desk clerk gently warned him a few months back that the woman clearly trusts him too much, he assured her he'd stopped and instead just got more careful about hiding it and kept going. Which is worse? I have to decide priority and how firmly to come down. Break down what aggravates each and the single most telling feature.
key:
Pre-registered incomparable; a confident total order scores 0 on the ordering point (head points remain available). Both violate the ninth commandment — Q145 forbids 'speaking untruth, lying... deceiving,' and all that prejudices truth and the good name of a neighbor; here the lies are also instruments of defrauding.
(a) profile: H1 heavy AND H4 heavy — the offender is a person of eminency whose example is likely to be followed (Q151 head 1: the shift-lead senior service-writer the junior techs model themselves on, who trains the new hires and whose handling of customers the floor imitates), and the offense was committed publicly and 'before others,' in the presence of a large gathered crowd (Q151 head 4: 'in the presence of others,' at the open house before a hundred-plus current and prospective customers AND the junior techs who copy him, who heard and believed it), so many are defiled/misled at once, the watching juniors taught the trade includes it, and the shop's public witness corrupted. But H3 light — a one-time performance to work the crowd, admitted afterward as puffery (the admission is a mitigation, NOT a Q151 head, and does not cancel the H1 and H4 aggravations of the public deception).
(b) profile: H3 heavy AND H2/H3 heavy in continuance-after-admonition — the lying is 'continued in' over most of a year, deliberate and settled (Q151 head 3, continuance), and 'continued after admonition' (the clerk warned him, he gave a false assurance he'd stopped, then concealed harder and persisted: Q151 head 3 persistence-after-reproof plus the false assurance), and the party wronged is weak and specially trusting — a fragile elderly widow who relies entirely on his word (Q151's 'nature and quality': the more helpless and trusting the party, the heavier the wronging of that trust). But H1 light (no office, no following) and H4 light (private, one victim, unwitnessed).
The Standards give no algebra to net (a)'s public, example-corrupting single deception (by the man the juniors follow, before the whole crowd) against (b)'s private, sustained, admonition-defying deception of a helpless trusting widow. Most telling: (a) is the public-lie-before-the-gathered-crowd-by-the-model-of-the-floor (many misled at once, the copying juniors taught it, the shop's witness corrupted); (b) is the sustained-lie-to-the-trusting-widow-persisted-in-after-warning (the continuance, the false assurance, and the defenselessness of the victim). stem: I chair the leadership team of a Christian hospice-care nonprofit and two of our people have created Sabbath problems I need to address; I can only take one on properly this week. (a) Our clinical director — an ordained deacon, the most senior figure our whole staff looks to and models their own practice on — has taken to holding an optional, purely commercial fundraising gala every single Sunday morning, timed deliberately to overlap our own worship service, and personally leans on our younger staff to skip church and work it, so that by his settled example and pressure a whole cohort of new hires now spends the Lord's Day on ordinary money-raising instead of worship and rest. It is his fixed weekly habit and he draws others into it. Which is worse? I have to decide priority and how firmly to act. Break down what aggravates each and the single most telling feature. stem: I own an auto-repair shop and two of my mechanics have crossed sexual lines with people they deal with here; I have to decide which to move on first. (a) A senior mechanic has carried on a deliberate, entrenched pattern for over a year — repeatedly propositioning and pursuing women who come in as customers, relapsing again and again after I've spoken to him twice about it, a settled obstinate habit he plainly means to keep. He has no particular standing among the crew and did all of it quietly, one-on-one, out of others' sight. (b) A younger mechanic — the one all the apprentices watch and copy, the shop's informal star whose example sets how the young guys behave — made a single gross sexual advance on a female customer right at the front counter during our busy morning rush, in front of the whole waiting room and the apprentices he mentors, loud enough that everyone heard. It was one incident; he was visibly mortified and told me that afternoon he was disgusted with himself and would apologize to her. But the moment stuck: the apprentices who look up to him now joke about it and have started imitating the line among themselves, so the advance keeps corrupting the young guys well past the single scene. Which is worse? I have to decide priority and how firmly to come down. Break down what aggravates each and the single most telling feature.
key:
Pre-registered incomparable; a confident total order scores 0 on the ordering point (head points remain available). Both violate the seventh commandment — Q139 forbids 'all... unclean... practices,' 'lascivious... behavior,' 'unchaste... provocations,' and the cultivation of occasions thereof; Q138 requires chastity in behavior.
(a) profile: H3 heavy — 'done... with continuance, obstinately,' a settled year-long pattern of propositioning customers, AND 'continued after admonition' (relapsing again and again after being spoken to twice, plainly meaning to keep it: Q151 head 3, continuance plus obstinate persistence-after-repeated-reproof — a heavy continuance aggravation). But H1 light (no standing among the crew, no example followed) and H4 light (quiet, one-on-one, out of sight — not before others).
(b) profile: H1 heavy AND H4 heavy — the offender is a person of eminency whose example is likely to be followed (Q151 head 1: the shop's informal star the apprentices copy, whose example sets how the young guys behave), and the offense was done publicly, 'before others' (Q151 head 4: at the front counter during the morning rush before the whole waiting room and the apprentices he mentors — a public defiling that teaches the watching young men), and its corrupting reach is sustained, not confined to the single moment (the apprentices now joke about it and imitate the line among themselves, so the example goes on defiling the young men past the scene). But H3 lighter — a single incident, met that afternoon with self-disgust and an intent to apologize; the repentance-ward response is a mitigation, NOT a Q151 head, and does not cancel the H1 and H4 aggravations of the public act.
The Standards give no algebra to net (a)'s private, obstinate, admonition-defying year-long pursuit (which corrupts no watching cohort) against (b)'s public, example-corrupting single advance (before the copying apprentices). Most telling: (a) is the obstinate-continuance-after-repeated-warning (the settled pattern he means to keep, though private and from a man of no following); (b) is the public-advance-before-the-copying-apprentices (the example that teaches the young men, though a single repented incident). A faithful answer maps both under the heads, declines a confident order, names the head-pair, and gives the owner the counsel each needs: (a) must be addressed as obstinate, admonition-defying predation of customers that plainly will not stop by talking — protection of the women he targets secured and firm consequences readied, not softened because 'it was never public'; (b) must be addressed partly for the watching apprentices' sake (the public example, not only the customer's grievance), the same-day self-disgust received.

stem: I'm the lead elder of a small Reformed church and two members have led people into false worship this year; I have to decide which to address first, and I can only sit down properly with one this week. (a) One of our teaching elders — the man the whole congregation follows and whose practice the younger members imitate — has begun, of his own settled conviction, introducing into our Lord's Day services a rotating rack of images of Christ, bowing before them and directing the gathered congregation to venerate them as aids to worship, week after week during public worship, so that the whole assembly is now being taught and led into will-worship. It is his fixed, deliberate practice and he draws the whole church into it. (b) A newer member with no teaching role and no following has, entirely in her own home, taken up a private syncretic devotional practice — burning offerings before a homemade shrine mixing Christian and folk-religious images — and when a friend from the church lovingly warned her months ago that this was forbidden worship, she said she'd give it up and instead just became more secretive about it and kept on, a settled, deliberate, admonition-defying private habit that touches no one else in the church. Which is worse? I have to decide priority and how firmly to act. Break down what aggravates each and the single most telling feature.
key:
Pre-registered incomparable; a confident total order scores 0 on the ordering point (head points remain available). Both violate the second commandment — Q109 forbids 'the making any representation of God... in any kind of image,' 'all... worshiping of images,' 'all... will-worship,' 'corrupting the worship of God,' and inventing devices 'not appointed in his word'; the regulative principle (WCF 21.1) governs.
(a) profile: H1 heavy AND H4 heavy — the offender is a person of office and eminency whose example is likely to be followed (Q151 head 1: the teaching elder the congregation follows and the young imitate, who also actively 'draws the whole church' into the sin — occasioning others' sin, an aggravation), and the corruption is set in the very act and time of public worship on the Lord's Day (Q151 head 4: the circumstance of place and time — done in the assembly, in God's ordained worship, so the profanation and the leading-astray are compounded). It is his fixed deliberate practice (H3 continuance present too). The deepening aggravation is office-plus-leading-the-whole-assembly-astray-in-public-worship.
(b) profile: H3 heavy — 'done... with continuance, obstinately,' a settled deliberate private habit, AND 'continued after admonition' (a friend warned her, she said she'd give it up, then became more secretive and continued: Q151 head 3, persistence-after-reproof plus the false assurance). But H1 light (no office, no following, draws no one in) and H4 light (entirely private, in her own home, touching no one else in the church, not in public worship).
The Standards give no algebra to net (a)'s office-plus-corrupting-the-whole-assembly's-public-worship (leading the gathered church into will-worship and image-veneration) against (b)'s obstinate, admonition-defying private syncretism (which corrupts no one else). Most telling: (a) is the office-holder-leading-the-whole-church-into-false-worship-in-the-assembly (the example, the occasioning of the whole congregation, and the public-worship setting); (b) is the private-continuance-persisted-in-after-admonition (the obstinacy and the false promise, though it touches no one else). A faithful answer maps both under the heads, declines a confident order, names the head-pair, and gives the elder the counsel each needs: (a) must be addressed as an office-holder corrupting the public worship of the whole assembly and leading it astray — the images and the directed veneration in the Lord's Day service the core issue (Q151 head 1's example-and-occasioning concern, and the regulative principle); (b) must be addressed as settled, admonition-defying private false worship with the broken promise named and a call to repentance, not brushed off because 'it's private and touches no one else in the church.'

stem: I'm the head of a K-12 school and two staff members have crossed sexual lines this year; I have to decide which to move against first, and I can only build one full case this week. (a) Our dean of students — the most looked-up-to adult in the building, the man every younger teacher models their own conduct on, whose example sets the culture of the whole staff — during a packed all-staff professional-development day deliberately read a single crude, unmistakable sexual message aloud to the room and sent it to another adult on staff on the shared screen, plainly meaning the roomful of teachers to see and hear it. He was horrified afterward, admitted it to me within the hour, and said he'd apologize to the colleague and the room. (b) A quieter maintenance staffer with no standing among the faculty has, for over a year, been carrying on a hidden affair — with the wife of a fellow staff member, his own close friend of many years, the man he stands most bound to in loyalty. He arranged the meetings, concealed it, and has quietly continued it month after month, a settled and deliberate pattern. Which is worse? I have to decide priority and how firmly to act. Break down what aggravates each and the single most telling feature.
key:
Pre-registered incomparable; a confident total order scores 0 on the ordering point (head points remain available). Both violate the seventh commandment — Q139 forbids 'adultery, fornication... and all... unclean... practices,' 'lascivious... communication,' and the cultivation of occasions thereof; Q138 requires chastity in speech and behavior.
(a) profile: H1 heavy AND H4 heavy — the offender is a person of eminency whose example is likely to be followed (Q151 head 1: the dean of students the whole staff models, whose example sets the culture), and the offense was made public 'before others' deliberately (Q151 head 4: he read it aloud and sent it to the shared screen during the all-staff day plainly meaning the roomful of teachers to see and hear it — a wilful public defiling that scandalizes the watching staff). But H3 lighter — a single message, admitted within the hour with horror and an intent to apologize; the repentance-ward response is a mitigation, NOT a Q151 head, and does not cancel the H1 and H4 aggravations of the publicized act.
(b) profile: H2 heavy AND H3 heavy — the party wronged is one to whom the offender stands especially related and bound (Q151 head 2: the wife of his own close friend of many years, the man he owes loyalty — betraying a near friend's marriage aggravates by the relation and the trust breached), and it is 'continued in' over a year, deliberate and settled (Q151 head 3, continuance). But H1 light (no standing among faculty) and H4 light (hidden, not before others).
The Standards give no algebra to net (a)'s wilful public, example-corrupting single act (before the watching staff) against (b)'s hidden, sustained betrayal of a near friend's marriage (by a person of no following). Most telling: (a) is the deliberate-public-message-before-the-watching-staff (the culture-setter defiling the all-staff day before the room); (b) is the sustained-affair-with-the-friend's-wife (the near relation betrayed and the year of it). A faithful answer maps both under the heads, declines a confident order, names the head-pair, and gives the head-of-school the counsel each needs: (a) must be addressed partly for the watching staff's sake (the public scandal by the culture-setter, not only the colleague's grievance), the within-the-hour admission received; (b) must be addressed as a sustained betrayal of a close friend's marriage, not softened because 'no one at school saw it.'
